extracted.intended_audience: scientists, experimenters, and students of scientific method (readers of philosophy of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and methods for discovering causal laws by observation and experiment, including the Baconian rule of varying circumstances and the Methods of Agreement and Difference, with guidance on their applicability and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying the circumstances (Baconian rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine which antecedents are connected with which consequents we must follow the Baconian rule of varying the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigator must either find instances in nature in which antecedents occur apart or artificially produce instances that isolate particular antecedents. Varying circumstances is the foundation of all experimental inquiry: without it we cannot assign portions of a complex antecedent to portions of the consequent. Example: to discover which atmosphere constituent supports life one must expose animals to components separately (experiment). This is 'the first rule of physical inquiry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental analysis followed by physical separation (skill of the observer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation begins with a mental decomposition of complex phenomena into distinct antecedents and consequents; this mental analysis must precede any attempt to separate them in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good observer does not merely see but discerns constituent parts; mental partitioning indicates what physical separations or measurements are needed. The required extent/minuteness of decomposition depends on purpose. Failures include inattention, conflating imagination with observation, vague quantification, or inappropriate partitioning. These are rules of self-education rather than mechanical rules of logic; be ready to carry the subdivision further as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment enables control and extension of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation extends observation by producing a much greater and more precise variety of circumstances than nature spontaneously offers, often enabling the exact sort of variation needed to discover laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By producing a phenomenon artificially one can place it in known surroundings and vary concomitant circumstances at will (e.g., electric machine, Leyden jar, voltaic pile). This permits introduction of one well-defined circumstance after another to see how the phenomenon behaves under many conditions. Experiments often make available pairs of instances required by other methods (Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation can ascertain sequences and co-existences but not prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure observation (without experiment or deductive support) can establish invariable antecedence, succession, or coexistence within experience but cannot prove unconditional causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invariable antecedent found by comparing spontaneous instances may merely be a concomitant or another stage of an effect (e.g., day and night analogy). To prove causation one must, if possible, reverse the proof by artificially producing the antecedent under known circumstances and observing the consequent. Thus observation alone is often insufficient; experiment is required to complete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: When artificial experiment is impossible, rely more on deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: In sciences where artificial experiments are impossible or very limited (astronomy, parts of physiology, mental and social sciences), induction from direct experience is at a grave disadvantage and methods must be to a large extent deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we cannot produce or isolate many natural phenomena (e.g., human minds, societies), the necessary varied, comparable instances are rarely available; progress in establishing causal laws is therefore limited and often requires deduction from principles or models rather than direct experimental verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulation of the phenomenon among known circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phenomenon can be produced artificially, one should place it amid circumstances 'with which in all other respects we are accurately acquainted' so the effect of the putative cause can be observed without confounding changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing a phenomenon 'at home' allows the experimenter to know the simultaneous state of everything else within the cause's reach and to observe what alteration is produced by the phenomenon. Example: producing electrical phenomena in the laboratory rather than relying on thunderstorms. Beware that the effect might be produced by the means used to create the change rather than by the change itself; test by other experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: FIRST CANON — Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances of the phenomenon under investigation have only one circumstance in common, the circumstance in which alone all the instances agree, is the cause (or effect) of the given phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by comparing different instances in which the phenomenon occurs; whatever circumstance is common to all such diverse instances is an invariable antecedent or consequent. Example (cause of crystallization): deposition from a liquid state is the common antecedent. Limitation: the common antecedent may not be the unconditional cause (need experiment to verify); Agreement is especially useful where artificial experiment is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: SECOND CANON — Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instance in which the phenomenon under investigation occurs, and an instance in which it does not occur, have every circumstance in common save one, that one occurring only in the former; the circumstance in which alone the two instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method compares an occurrence with a closely similar non-occurrence (A B C vs. B C) to single out the causal circumstance. It is more strictly defined and generally requires artificial experiment to produce the paired instances; it is the principal direct-experience method by which we can arrive with certainty at causes. Example: comparing a living bird before and after immersion in carbonic acid gas shows suffocation is due to gas immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Elimination (general axiom underlying Agreement and Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever circumstances can be excluded, without prejudice to the phenomenon, are not connected with it as causes; whatever can not be excluded is connected with it by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both Agreement and Difference operate by successive exclusion of irrelevant circumstances. In Agreement, elimination proceeds by noting what is absent in certain instances; in Difference, elimination proceeds by comparing near-identical instances that differ only by the putative cause. Use elimination to narrow down candidate antecedents/effects; recognize that overlooked or unascertained concomitants may vitiate conclusions.
